turns.t: Sorry, sorry, we're late, the bus, and then Callum needed the toilet, and then I forgot the red book, so I've no idea what I've got here. ~
No worries at all. Come in, sit down. Hello Callum, how old are you? ~
Four! ~
Four, brilliant. Dad, tell me what's been going on. ~
Right, so. He was sick in the night, Tuesday, no, Wednesday, it was bin day so Wednesday, and he's been sick three times. And then this morning the runs started.
So vomiting since Wednesday night, and diarrhoea since this morning?
Yes. Well, the diarrhoea, it was before breakfast. Four times already today. Which is a lot for one small person.
Tummy hurts. ~
Does it, Callum? Show me where. ~
Here. ~
Okay. Is he drinking, Dad? ~
Little sips. He keeps asking for apple juice, and I've been, I don't know if I should be giving him that. ~
A few sips of whatever he'll take is fine. What about wees, is he still having wet nappies, or pants, I mean, sorry? ~
Yes, I think so. Twice today, I'd say. Yes. His brother had it last week, it's going round the nursery. ~
That helps me, thank you. Has Callum got any health problems I should know about?
He has asthma, mild, he's got the brown inhaler for it. Well, he had it, I'm not sure where it went.
That's fine, we can sort that out another day. Let's have a look at him. Can I take your temperature, Callum? ~
Under my arm? ~
Under your arm, you've done this before.
Is he warm? ~
Temperature 37.6, so just slightly raised, and his pulse is 108, which is normal for a four-year-old who's been vomiting.
Is that good? I never know what's good. ~
It's reassuring. Callum, lie back on the bed, I'm going to press your tummy. Tell me if it's sore. ~
Tickles! ~
His belly is soft, and he's not tender anywhere. There's nothing that worries me.
So what is it? ~
Together with the nursery and his brother, this looks like a tummy bug, gastroenteritis.
Does he need antibiotics? My mum says he'll need antibiotics. ~
No, they don't help with a stomach bug. What helps is fluids, a little and often. A few sips every few minutes rather than a big glass.
Little and often. I can do that. And food? ~
Plain, simple food when he asks for it. Nothing fatty. Don't force it. ~
Right. How long does it last? ~
Most children are right within three to five days. If the diarrhoea is still going after a week, I'd like you to bring in a stool sample so we can test it.
In a pot? ~
In a pot, yes. We'll give you one at reception. ~
Okay. And when do I worry? ~
If he's not weeing for eight hours, is very drowsy, vomits green, or has blood in the poo, take him to the emergency department.
Got it. I'll write it on my hand. ~
Good idea. Bye, Callum. ~
Bye! ~

chief_complaint.value: He was sick in the night

clinical_actions.description: Advise little and often fluids and plain food
Safety-net: go to emergency department if no wee for eight hours, drowsy, green vomit or blood in poo
